69:

Agents

70:

Agents are specialized AI assistants that can be configured for specific tasks and workflows. They allow you to create focused tools with custom prompts, models, and tool access.

71:
72:
Tip
73:

Use the plan agent to analyze code and review suggestions without making any code changes.

74:
75:

You can switch between agents during a session or invoke them with the @ mention.

76:
77:

Types

78:

There are two types of agents in OpenCode; primary agents and subagents.

79:
80:

Primary agents

81:

Primary agents are the main assistants you interact with directly. You can cycle through them using the Tab key, or your configured switch_agent keybind. These agents handle your main conversation. Tool access is configured via permissions — for example, Build has all tools enabled while Plan is restricted.

82:
83:
Tip
84:

You can use the Tab key to switch between primary agents during a session.

85:
86:

OpenCode comes with two built-in primary agents, Build and Plan. We'll 87: look at these below.

88:
89:

Subagents

90:

Subagents are specialized assistants that primary agents can invoke for specific tasks. You can also manually invoke them by @ mentioning them in your messages.

91:

OpenCode comes with three built-in subagents, General, Explore, and Scout. We'll look at this below.

92:
93:

Built-in

94:

OpenCode comes with two built-in primary agents and three built-in subagents.

95:
96:

Use build

97:

Mode: primary

98:

Build is the default primary agent with all tools enabled. This is the standard agent for development work where you need full access to file operations and system commands.

99:
100:

Use plan

101:

Mode: primary

102:

A restricted agent designed for planning and analysis. We use a permission system to give you more control and prevent unintended changes. 103: By default, all of the following are set to ask:

104:
    105:
  • file edits: All writes, patches, and edits
    • 106:
  • bash: All bash commands
    • 107:
108:

This agent is useful when you want the LLM to analyze code, suggest changes, or create plans without making any actual modifications to your codebase.

109:
110:

Use general

111:

Mode: subagent

112:

A general-purpose agent for researching complex questions and executing multi-step tasks. Has full tool access (except todo), so it can make file changes when needed. Use this to run multiple units of work in parallel.

113:
114:

Use explore

115:

Mode: subagent

116:

A fast, read-only agent for exploring codebases. Cannot modify files. Use this when you need to quickly find files by patterns, search code for keywords, or answer questions about the codebase.

117:
118:

Use scout

119:

Mode: subagent

120:

A read-only agent for external docs and dependency research. Use this when you need to clone a dependency repository into OpenCode's managed cache, inspect library source, or cross-reference local code against upstream implementations without modifying your workspace.

121:
122:

Use compaction

123:

Mode: primary

124:

Hidden system agent that compacts long context into a smaller summary. It runs automatically when needed and is not selectable in the UI.

125:
126:

Use title

127:

Mode: primary

128:

Hidden system agent that generates short session titles. It runs automatically and is not selectable in the UI.

129:
130:

Use summary

131:

Mode: primary

132:

Hidden system agent that creates session summaries. It runs automatically and is not selectable in the UI.

133:
134:

Usage

135:
    136:
  1. 137:

    For primary agents, use the Tab key to cycle through them during a session. You can also use your configured switch_agent keybind.

    138:
    2. 139:
  2. 140:

    Subagents can be invoked: 141: - Automatically by primary agents for specialized tasks based on their descriptions. 142: - Manually by @ mentioning a subagent in your message. For example.

    143:

    txt 144: @general help me search for this function

    145:
    3. 146:
  3. 147:

    Navigation between sessions: When subagents create child sessions, use session_child_first (default: \+Down) to enter the first child session from the parent.

    148:
    4. 149:
  4. 150:

    Once you are in a child session, use: 151: - session_child_cycle (default: Right) to cycle to the next child session 152: - session_child_cycle_reverse (default: Left) to cycle to the previous child session 153: - session_parent (default: Up) to return to the parent session

    154:
    5. 155:
156:

This lets you switch between the main conversation and specialized subagent work.

157:
158:

Configure

159:

You can customize the built-in agents or create your own through configuration. Agents can be configured in two ways:

160:
161:

JSON

162:

Configure agents in your opencode.json config file:

163: 
{
164:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
165:   "agent": {
166:     "build": {
167:       "mode": "primary",
168:       "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
169:       "prompt": "{file:./prompts/build.txt}",
170:       "permission": {
171:         "edit": "allow",
172:         "bash": "allow"
173:       }
174:     },
175:     "plan": {
176:       "mode": "primary",
177:       "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-20250514",
178:       "permission": {
179:         "edit": "deny",
180:         "bash": "deny"
181:       }
182:     },
183:     "code-reviewer": {
184:       "description": "Reviews code for best practices and potential issues",
185:       "mode": "subagent",
186:       "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
187:       "prompt": "You are a code reviewer. Focus on security, performance, and maintainability.",
188:       "permission": {
189:         "edit": "deny"
190:       }
191:     }
192:   }
193: }
194:
195:
196:

Markdown

197:

You can also define agents using markdown files. Place them in:

198:
    199:
  • Global: ~/.config/opencode/agents/
    • 200:
  • Per-project: .opencode/agents/
    • 201:
202: 
---
203: description: Reviews code for quality and best practices
204: mode: subagent
205: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514
206: temperature: 0.1
207: permission:
208:   edit: deny
209:   bash: deny
210: ---
211: 
212: You are in code review mode. Focus on:
213: 
214: - Code quality and best practices
215: - Potential bugs and edge cases
216: - Performance implications
217: - Security considerations
218: 
219: Provide constructive feedback without making direct changes.
220:
221:

The markdown file name becomes the agent name. For example, review.md creates a review agent.

222:
223:

Options

224:

Let's look at these configuration options in detail.

225:
226:

Description

227:

Use the description option to provide a brief description of what the agent does and when to use it.

228: 
{
229:   "agent": {
230:     "review": {
231:       "description": "Reviews code for best practices and potential issues"
232:     }
233:   }
234: }
235:
236:

This is a required config option.

237:
238:

Temperature

239:

Control the randomness and creativity of the LLM's responses with the temperature config.

240:

Lower values make responses more focused and deterministic, while higher values increase creativity and variability.

241: 
{
242:   "agent": {
243:     "plan": {
244:       "temperature": 0.1
245:     },
246:     "creative": {
247:       "temperature": 0.8
248:     }
249:   }
250: }
251:
252:

Temperature values typically range from 0.0 to 1.0:

253:
    254:
  • 0.0-0.2: Very focused and deterministic responses, ideal for code analysis and planning
    • 255:
  • 0.3-0.5: Balanced responses with some creativity, good for general development tasks
    • 256:
  • 0.6-1.0: More creative and varied responses, useful for brainstorming and exploration
    • 257:
258: 
{
259:   "agent": {
260:     "analyze": {
261:       "temperature": 0.1,
262:       "prompt": "{file:./prompts/analysis.txt}"
263:     },
264:     "build": {
265:       "temperature": 0.3
266:     },
267:     "brainstorm": {
268:       "temperature": 0.7,
269:       "prompt": "{file:./prompts/creative.txt}"
270:     }
271:   }
272: }
273:
274:

If no temperature is specified, OpenCode uses model-specific defaults; typically 0 for most models, 0.55 for Qwen models.

275:
276:

Max steps

277:

Control the maximum number of agentic iterations an agent can perform before being forced to respond with text only. This allows users who wish to control costs to set a limit on agentic actions.

278:

If this is not set, the agent will continue to iterate until the model chooses to stop or the user interrupts the session.

279: 
{
280:   "agent": {
281:     "quick-thinker": {
282:       "description": "Fast reasoning with limited iterations",
283:       "prompt": "You are a quick thinker. Solve problems with minimal steps.",
284:       "steps": 5
285:     }
286:   }
287: }
288:
289:

When the limit is reached, the agent receives a special system prompt instructing it to respond with a summarization of its work and recommended remaining tasks.

290:
291:
Caution
292:

The legacy maxSteps field is deprecated. Use steps instead.

293:
294:
295:

Disable

296:

Set to true to disable the agent.

297: 
{
298:   "agent": {
299:     "review": {
300:       "disable": true
301:     }
302:   }
303: }
304:
305:
306:

Prompt

307:

Specify a custom system prompt file for this agent with the prompt config. The prompt file should contain instructions specific to the agent's purpose.

308: 
{
309:   "agent": {
310:     "review": {
311:       "prompt": "{file:./prompts/code-review.txt}"
312:     }
313:   }
314: }
315:
316:

This path is relative to where the config file is located. So this works for both the global OpenCode config and the project specific config.

317:
318:

Model

319:

Use the model config to override the model for this agent. Useful for using different models optimized for different tasks. For example, a faster model for planning, a more capable model for implementation.

320:
321:
Tip
322:

If you don’t specify a model, primary agents use the model globally configured while subagents will use the model of the primary agent that invoked the subagent.

323:
324: 
{
325:   "agent": {
326:     "plan": {
327:       "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-20250514"
328:     }
329:   }
330: }
331:
332:

The model ID in your OpenCode config uses the format provider/model-id. For example, if you're using OpenCode Zen, you would use opencode/gpt-5.1-codex for GPT 5.1 Codex.

333:
334:

Tools (deprecated)

335:

tools is deprecated. Prefer the agent's permission field for new configs, updates and more fine-grained control.

336:

Allows you to control which tools are available in this agent. You can enable or disable specific tools by setting them to true or false. In an agent's tools config, true is equivalent to {"*": "allow"} permission and false is equivalent to {"*": "deny"} permission.

337: 
{
338:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
339:   "tools": {
340:     "write": true,
341:     "bash": true
342:   },
343:   "agent": {
344:     "plan": {
345:       "tools": {
346:         "write": false,
347:         "bash": false
348:       }
349:     }
350:   }
351: }
352:
353:
354:
Note
355:

The agent-specific config overrides the global config.

356:
357:

You can also use wildcards in legacy tools entries to control multiple tools at once. For example, to disable all tools from an MCP server:

358: 
{
359:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
360:   "agent": {
361:     "readonly": {
362:       "tools": {
363:         "mymcp_*": false,
364:         "write": false,
365:         "edit": false
366:       }
367:     }
368:   }
369: }
370:
371:

Learn more about tools.

372:
373:

Permissions

374:

You can configure permissions to manage what actions an agent can take. Each permission key can be set to:

375:
    376:
  • "ask" — Prompt for approval before running the tool
    • 377:
  • "allow" — Allow all operations without approval
    • 378:
  • "deny" — Disable the tool
    • 379:
380:

The available permission keys are:

381: 382: 383: 384: 385: 386: 387: 388: 389: 390: 391: 392: 393: 394: 395: 396: 397: 398: 399: 400: 401: 402: 403: 404: 405: 406: 407: 408: 409: 410: 411: 412: 413: 414: 415: 416: 417: 418: 419: 420: 421: 422: 423: 424: 425: 426: 427: 428: 429: 430: 431: 432: 433: 434: 435: 436: 437: 438: 439: 440: 441: 442: 443: 444: 445: 446: 447: 448: 449: 450:
KeyTools it gates
readread
editwrite, edit, apply_patch
globglob
grepgrep
listlist
bashbash
tasktask
external_directoryAny tool that reads or writes files outside the project worktree
todowritetodowrite, todoread
webfetchwebfetch
websearchwebsearch
lsplsp
skillskill
questionquestion
doom_loopRecovery prompts when an agent appears stuck
451:

read, edit, glob, grep, list, bash, task, external_directory, lsp, and skill accept either a shorthand action ("allow" | "ask" | "deny") or an object of glob/pattern → action for fine-grained control. The remaining keys accept the shorthand action only.

452:
453:
Note
454:

Permission keys are matched as wildcard patterns against the underlying tool name, so the same syntax works for built-ins, custom tools, and MCP tools — for example "mymcp_*": "deny" denies every tool from an MCP server, and "mymcp_search": "ask" targets a single one.

455:
456: 
{
457:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
458:   "permission": {
459:     "edit": "deny"
460:   }
461: }
462:
463:

You can override these permissions per agent.

464: 
{
465:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
466:   "permission": {
467:     "edit": "deny"
468:   },
469:   "agent": {
470:     "build": {
471:       "permission": {
472:         "edit": "ask"
473:       }
474:     }
475:   }
476: }
477:
478:

You can also set permissions in Markdown agents.

479: 
---
480: description: Code review without edits
481: mode: subagent
482: permission:
483:   edit: deny
484:   bash:
485:     "*": ask
486:     "git diff": allow
487:     "git log*": allow
488:     "grep *": allow
489:   webfetch: deny
490: ---
491: 
492: Only analyze code and suggest changes.
493:
494:

You can set permissions for specific bash commands.

495: 
{
496:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
497:   "agent": {
498:     "build": {
499:       "permission": {
500:         "bash": {
501:           "git push": "ask",
502:           "grep *": "allow"
503:         }
504:       }
505:     }
506:   }
507: }
508:
509:

This can take a glob pattern.

510: 
{
511:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
512:   "agent": {
513:     "build": {
514:       "permission": {
515:         "bash": {
516:           "git *": "ask"
517:         }
518:       }
519:     }
520:   }
521: }
522:
523:

And you can also use the * wildcard to manage permissions for all commands. 524: Since the last matching rule takes precedence, put the * wildcard first and specific rules after.

525: 
{
526:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
527:   "agent": {
528:     "build": {
529:       "permission": {
530:         "bash": {
531:           "*": "ask",
532:           "git status *": "allow"
533:         }
534:       }
535:     }
536:   }
537: }
538:
539:

Learn more about permissions.

540:
541:

Mode

542:

Control the agent's mode with the mode config. The mode option is used to determine how the agent can be used.

543: 
{
544:   "agent": {
545:     "review": {
546:       "mode": "subagent"
547:     }
548:   }
549: }
550:
551:

The mode option can be set to primary, subagent, or all. If no mode is specified, it defaults to all.

552:
553:

Hidden

554:

Hide a subagent from the @ autocomplete menu with hidden: true. Useful for internal subagents that should only be invoked programmatically by other agents via the Task tool.

555: 
{
556:   "agent": {
557:     "internal-helper": {
558:       "mode": "subagent",
559:       "hidden": true
560:     }
561:   }
562: }
563:
564:

This only affects user visibility in the autocomplete menu. Hidden agents can still be invoked by the model via the Task tool if permissions allow.

565:
566:
Note
567:

Only applies to mode: subagent agents.

568:
569:
570:

Task permissions

571:

Control which subagents an agent can invoke via the Task tool with permission.task. Uses glob patterns for flexible matching.

572: 
{
573:   "agent": {
574:     "orchestrator": {
575:       "mode": "primary",
576:       "permission": {
577:         "task": {
578:           "*": "deny",
579:           "orchestrator-*": "allow",
580:           "code-reviewer": "ask"
581:         }
582:       }
583:     }
584:   }
585: }
586:
587:

When set to deny, the subagent is removed from the Task tool description entirely, so the model won't attempt to invoke it.

588:
589:
Tip
590:

Rules are evaluated in order, and the last matching rule wins. In the example above, orchestrator-planner matches both * (deny) and orchestrator-* (allow), but since orchestrator-* comes after *, the result is allow.

591:
592:
593:
Tip
594:

Users can always invoke any subagent directly via the @ autocomplete menu, even if the agent's task permissions would deny it.

595:
596:
597:

Color

598:

Customize the agent's visual appearance in the UI with the color option. This affects how the agent appears in the interface.

599:

Use a valid hex color (e.g., #FF5733) or theme color: primary, secondary, accent, success, warning, error, info.

600: 
{
601:   "agent": {
602:     "creative": {
603:       "color": "#ff6b6b"
604:     },
605:     "code-reviewer": {
606:       "color": "accent"
607:     }
608:   }
609: }
610:
611:
612:

Top P

613:

Control response diversity with the top_p option. Alternative to temperature for controlling randomness.

614: 
{
615:   "agent": {
616:     "brainstorm": {
617:       "top_p": 0.9
618:     }
619:   }
620: }
621:
622:

Values range from 0.0 to 1.0. Lower values are more focused, higher values more diverse.

623:
624:

Additional

625:

Any other options you specify in your agent configuration will be passed through directly to the provider as model options. This allows you to use provider-specific features and parameters.

626:

For example, with OpenAI's reasoning models, you can control the reasoning effort:

627: 
{
628:   "agent": {
629:     "deep-thinker": {
630:       "description": "Agent that uses high reasoning effort for complex problems",
631:       "model": "openai/gpt-5",
632:       "reasoningEffort": "high",
633:       "textVerbosity": "low"
634:     }
635:   }
636: }
637:
638:

These additional options are model and provider-specific. Check your provider's documentation for available parameters.

639:
640:
Tip
641:

Run opencode models to see a list of the available models.

642:
643:
644:

Create agents

645:

You can create new agents using the following command:

646: 
opencode agent create
647:
648:

This interactive command will:

649:
    650:
  1. Ask where to save the agent; global or project-specific.
    2. 651:
  2. Description of what the agent should do.
    3. 652:
  3. Generate an appropriate system prompt and identifier.
    4. 653:
  4. Let you select which permissions the agent should be allowed (anything you don't select is denied).
    5. 654:
  5. Finally, create a markdown file with the agent configuration.
    6. 655:
656:
657:

Use cases

658:

Here are some common use cases for different agents.

659:
    660:
  • Build agent: Full development work with all tools enabled
    • 661:
  • Plan agent: Analysis and planning without making changes
    • 662:
  • Review agent: Code review with read-only access plus documentation tools
    • 663:
  • Debug agent: Focused on investigation with bash and read tools enabled
    • 664:
  • Docs agent: Documentation writing with file operations but no system commands
    • 665:
666:
667:

Examples

668:

Here are some example agents you might find useful.

669:
670:
Tip
671:

Do you have an agent you'd like to share? Submit a PR.

672:
673:
674:

Documentation agent

675: 
---
676: description: Writes and maintains project documentation
677: mode: subagent
678: permission:
679:   bash: deny
680: ---
681: 
682: You are a technical writer. Create clear, comprehensive documentation.
683: 
684: Focus on:
685: 
686: - Clear explanations
687: - Proper structure
688: - Code examples
689: - User-friendly language
690:
691:
692:

Security auditor

693: 
---
694: description: Performs security audits and identifies vulnerabilities
695: mode: subagent
696: permission:
697:   edit: deny
698: ---
699: 
700: You are a security expert. Focus on identifying potential security issues.
701: 
702: Look for:
703: 
704: - Input validation vulnerabilities
705: - Authentication and authorization flaws
706: - Data exposure risks

OpenCode 1.18.25 docs Introduction ACP Support Agent Skills Agents CLI Commands Config Custom Tools Ecosystem Enterprise Formatters GitHub GitLab Go IDE Keybinds LSP Servers MCP servers Models Network Permissions Plugins Policies Providers References Rules SDK Server Share Themes Tools Troubleshooting TUI Web Windows (WSL) Zen

Agents

Agents are specialized AI assistants that can be configured for specific tasks and workflows. They allow you to create focused tools with custom prompts, models, and tool access.

Tip

Use the plan agent to analyze code and review suggestions without making any code changes.

You can switch between agents during a session or invoke them with the @ mention.

Types

There are two types of agents in OpenCode; primary agents and subagents.

Primary agents

Primary agents are the main assistants you interact with directly. You can cycle through them using the Tab key, or your configured switch_agent keybind. These agents handle your main conversation. Tool access is configured via permissions — for example, Build has all tools enabled while Plan is restricted.

Tip

You can use the Tab key to switch between primary agents during a session.

OpenCode comes with two built-in primary agents, Build and Plan. We'll look at these below.

Subagents

Subagents are specialized assistants that primary agents can invoke for specific tasks. You can also manually invoke them by @ mentioning them in your messages.

OpenCode comes with three built-in subagents, General, Explore, and Scout. We'll look at this below.

Built-in

OpenCode comes with two built-in primary agents and three built-in subagents.

Use build

Mode: primary

Build is the default primary agent with all tools enabled. This is the standard agent for development work where you need full access to file operations and system commands.

Use plan

Mode: primary

A restricted agent designed for planning and analysis. We use a permission system to give you more control and prevent unintended changes. By default, all of the following are set to ask:

  • file edits: All writes, patches, and edits
  • bash: All bash commands

This agent is useful when you want the LLM to analyze code, suggest changes, or create plans without making any actual modifications to your codebase.

Use general

Mode: subagent

A general-purpose agent for researching complex questions and executing multi-step tasks. Has full tool access (except todo), so it can make file changes when needed. Use this to run multiple units of work in parallel.

Use explore

Mode: subagent

A fast, read-only agent for exploring codebases. Cannot modify files. Use this when you need to quickly find files by patterns, search code for keywords, or answer questions about the codebase.

Use scout

Mode: subagent

A read-only agent for external docs and dependency research. Use this when you need to clone a dependency repository into OpenCode's managed cache, inspect library source, or cross-reference local code against upstream implementations without modifying your workspace.

Use compaction

Mode: primary

Hidden system agent that compacts long context into a smaller summary. It runs automatically when needed and is not selectable in the UI.

Use title

Mode: primary

Hidden system agent that generates short session titles. It runs automatically and is not selectable in the UI.

Use summary

Mode: primary

Hidden system agent that creates session summaries. It runs automatically and is not selectable in the UI.

Usage

  1. For primary agents, use the Tab key to cycle through them during a session. You can also use your configured switch_agent keybind.

  2. Subagents can be invoked: - Automatically by primary agents for specialized tasks based on their descriptions. - Manually by @ mentioning a subagent in your message. For example.

    txt @general help me search for this function

  3. Navigation between sessions: When subagents create child sessions, use session_child_first (default: \+Down) to enter the first child session from the parent.

  4. Once you are in a child session, use: - session_child_cycle (default: Right) to cycle to the next child session - session_child_cycle_reverse (default: Left) to cycle to the previous child session - session_parent (default: Up) to return to the parent session

This lets you switch between the main conversation and specialized subagent work.

Configure

You can customize the built-in agents or create your own through configuration. Agents can be configured in two ways:

JSON

Configure agents in your opencode.json config file:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agent": {
    "build": {
      "mode": "primary",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
      "prompt": "{file:./prompts/build.txt}",
      "permission": {
        "edit": "allow",
        "bash": "allow"
      }
    },
    "plan": {
      "mode": "primary",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-20250514",
      "permission": {
        "edit": "deny",
        "bash": "deny"
      }
    },
    "code-reviewer": {
      "description": "Reviews code for best practices and potential issues",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
      "prompt": "You are a code reviewer. Focus on security, performance, and maintainability.",
      "permission": {
        "edit": "deny"
      }
    }
  }
}

Markdown

You can also define agents using markdown files. Place them in:

  • Global: ~/.config/opencode/agents/
  • Per-project: .opencode/agents/
---
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices
mode: subagent
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514
temperature: 0.1
permission:
  edit: deny
  bash: deny
---

You are in code review mode. Focus on:

- Code quality and best practices
- Potential bugs and edge cases
- Performance implications
- Security considerations

Provide constructive feedback without making direct changes.

The markdown file name becomes the agent name. For example, review.md creates a review agent.

Options

Let's look at these configuration options in detail.

Description

Use the description option to provide a brief description of what the agent does and when to use it.

{
  "agent": {
    "review": {
      "description": "Reviews code for best practices and potential issues"
    }
  }
}

This is a required config option.

Temperature

Control the randomness and creativity of the LLM's responses with the temperature config.

Lower values make responses more focused and deterministic, while higher values increase creativity and variability.

{
  "agent": {
    "plan": {
      "temperature": 0.1
    },
    "creative": {
      "temperature": 0.8
    }
  }
}

Temperature values typically range from 0.0 to 1.0:

  • 0.0-0.2: Very focused and deterministic responses, ideal for code analysis and planning
  • 0.3-0.5: Balanced responses with some creativity, good for general development tasks
  • 0.6-1.0: More creative and varied responses, useful for brainstorming and exploration
{
  "agent": {
    "analyze": {
      "temperature": 0.1,
      "prompt": "{file:./prompts/analysis.txt}"
    },
    "build": {
      "temperature": 0.3
    },
    "brainstorm": {
      "temperature": 0.7,
      "prompt": "{file:./prompts/creative.txt}"
    }
  }
}

If no temperature is specified, OpenCode uses model-specific defaults; typically 0 for most models, 0.55 for Qwen models.

Max steps

Control the maximum number of agentic iterations an agent can perform before being forced to respond with text only. This allows users who wish to control costs to set a limit on agentic actions.

If this is not set, the agent will continue to iterate until the model chooses to stop or the user interrupts the session.

{
  "agent": {
    "quick-thinker": {
      "description": "Fast reasoning with limited iterations",
      "prompt": "You are a quick thinker. Solve problems with minimal steps.",
      "steps": 5
    }
  }
}

When the limit is reached, the agent receives a special system prompt instructing it to respond with a summarization of its work and recommended remaining tasks.

Caution

The legacy maxSteps field is deprecated. Use steps instead.

Disable

Set to true to disable the agent.

{
  "agent": {
    "review": {
      "disable": true
    }
  }
}

Prompt

Specify a custom system prompt file for this agent with the prompt config. The prompt file should contain instructions specific to the agent's purpose.

{
  "agent": {
    "review": {
      "prompt": "{file:./prompts/code-review.txt}"
    }
  }
}

This path is relative to where the config file is located. So this works for both the global OpenCode config and the project specific config.

Model

Use the model config to override the model for this agent. Useful for using different models optimized for different tasks. For example, a faster model for planning, a more capable model for implementation.

Tip

If you don’t specify a model, primary agents use the model globally configured while subagents will use the model of the primary agent that invoked the subagent.

{
  "agent": {
    "plan": {
      "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-20250514"
    }
  }
}

The model ID in your OpenCode config uses the format provider/model-id. For example, if you're using OpenCode Zen, you would use opencode/gpt-5.1-codex for GPT 5.1 Codex.

Tools (deprecated)

tools is deprecated. Prefer the agent's permission field for new configs, updates and more fine-grained control.

Allows you to control which tools are available in this agent. You can enable or disable specific tools by setting them to true or false. In an agent's tools config, true is equivalent to {"*": "allow"} permission and false is equivalent to {"*": "deny"} permission.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "tools": {
    "write": true,
    "bash": true
  },
  "agent": {
    "plan": {
      "tools": {
        "write": false,
        "bash": false
      }
    }
  }
}
Note

The agent-specific config overrides the global config.

You can also use wildcards in legacy tools entries to control multiple tools at once. For example, to disable all tools from an MCP server:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agent": {
    "readonly": {
      "tools": {
        "mymcp_*": false,
        "write": false,
        "edit": false
      }
    }
  }
}

Learn more about tools.

Permissions

You can configure permissions to manage what actions an agent can take. Each permission key can be set to:

  • "ask" — Prompt for approval before running the tool
  • "allow" — Allow all operations without approval
  • "deny" — Disable the tool

The available permission keys are:

Key Tools it gates
read read
edit write, edit, apply_patch
glob glob
grep grep
list list
bash bash
task task
external_directory Any tool that reads or writes files outside the project worktree
todowrite todowrite, todoread
webfetch webfetch
websearch websearch
lsp lsp
skill skill
question question
doom_loop Recovery prompts when an agent appears stuck

read, edit, glob, grep, list, bash, task, external_directory, lsp, and skill accept either a shorthand action ("allow" | "ask" | "deny") or an object of glob/pattern → action for fine-grained control. The remaining keys accept the shorthand action only.

Note

Permission keys are matched as wildcard patterns against the underlying tool name, so the same syntax works for built-ins, custom tools, and MCP tools — for example "mymcp_*": "deny" denies every tool from an MCP server, and "mymcp_search": "ask" targets a single one.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permission": {
    "edit": "deny"
  }
}

You can override these permissions per agent.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permission": {
    "edit": "deny"
  },
  "agent": {
    "build": {
      "permission": {
        "edit": "ask"
      }
    }
  }
}

You can also set permissions in Markdown agents.

---
description: Code review without edits
mode: subagent
permission:
  edit: deny
  bash:
    "*": ask
    "git diff": allow
    "git log*": allow
    "grep *": allow
  webfetch: deny
---

Only analyze code and suggest changes.

You can set permissions for specific bash commands.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agent": {
    "build": {
      "permission": {
        "bash": {
          "git push": "ask",
          "grep *": "allow"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

This can take a glob pattern.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agent": {
    "build": {
      "permission": {
        "bash": {
          "git *": "ask"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

And you can also use the * wildcard to manage permissions for all commands. Since the last matching rule takes precedence, put the * wildcard first and specific rules after.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agent": {
    "build": {
      "permission": {
        "bash": {
          "*": "ask",
          "git status *": "allow"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Learn more about permissions.

Mode

Control the agent's mode with the mode config. The mode option is used to determine how the agent can be used.

{
  "agent": {
    "review": {
      "mode": "subagent"
    }
  }
}

The mode option can be set to primary, subagent, or all. If no mode is specified, it defaults to all.

Hidden

Hide a subagent from the @ autocomplete menu with hidden: true. Useful for internal subagents that should only be invoked programmatically by other agents via the Task tool.

{
  "agent": {
    "internal-helper": {
      "mode": "subagent",
      "hidden": true
    }
  }
}

This only affects user visibility in the autocomplete menu. Hidden agents can still be invoked by the model via the Task tool if permissions allow.

Note

Only applies to mode: subagent agents.

Task permissions

Control which subagents an agent can invoke via the Task tool with permission.task. Uses glob patterns for flexible matching.

{
  "agent": {
    "orchestrator": {
      "mode": "primary",
      "permission": {
        "task": {
          "*": "deny",
          "orchestrator-*": "allow",
          "code-reviewer": "ask"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

When set to deny, the subagent is removed from the Task tool description entirely, so the model won't attempt to invoke it.

Tip

Rules are evaluated in order, and the last matching rule wins. In the example above, orchestrator-planner matches both * (deny) and orchestrator-* (allow), but since orchestrator-* comes after *, the result is allow.

Tip

Users can always invoke any subagent directly via the @ autocomplete menu, even if the agent's task permissions would deny it.

Color

Customize the agent's visual appearance in the UI with the color option. This affects how the agent appears in the interface.

Use a valid hex color (e.g., #FF5733) or theme color: primary, secondary, accent, success, warning, error, info.

{
  "agent": {
    "creative": {
      "color": "#ff6b6b"
    },
    "code-reviewer": {
      "color": "accent"
    }
  }
}

Top P

Control response diversity with the top_p option. Alternative to temperature for controlling randomness.

{
  "agent": {
    "brainstorm": {
      "top_p": 0.9
    }
  }
}

Values range from 0.0 to 1.0. Lower values are more focused, higher values more diverse.

Additional

Any other options you specify in your agent configuration will be passed through directly to the provider as model options. This allows you to use provider-specific features and parameters.

For example, with OpenAI's reasoning models, you can control the reasoning effort:

{
  "agent": {
    "deep-thinker": {
      "description": "Agent that uses high reasoning effort for complex problems",
      "model": "openai/gpt-5",
      "reasoningEffort": "high",
      "textVerbosity": "low"
    }
  }
}

These additional options are model and provider-specific. Check your provider's documentation for available parameters.

Tip

Run opencode models to see a list of the available models.

Create agents

You can create new agents using the following command:

opencode agent create

This interactive command will:

  1. Ask where to save the agent; global or project-specific.
  2. Description of what the agent should do.
  3. Generate an appropriate system prompt and identifier.
  4. Let you select which permissions the agent should be allowed (anything you don't select is denied).
  5. Finally, create a markdown file with the agent configuration.

Use cases

Here are some common use cases for different agents.

  • Build agent: Full development work with all tools enabled
  • Plan agent: Analysis and planning without making changes
  • Review agent: Code review with read-only access plus documentation tools
  • Debug agent: Focused on investigation with bash and read tools enabled
  • Docs agent: Documentation writing with file operations but no system commands

Examples

Here are some example agents you might find useful.

Tip

Do you have an agent you'd like to share? Submit a PR.

Documentation agent

---
description: Writes and maintains project documentation
mode: subagent
permission:
  bash: deny
---

You are a technical writer. Create clear, comprehensive documentation.

Focus on:

- Clear explanations
- Proper structure
- Code examples
- User-friendly language

Security auditor

---
description: Performs security audits and identifies vulnerabilities
mode: subagent
permission:
  edit: deny
---

You are a security expert. Focus on identifying potential security issues.

Look for:

- Input validation vulnerabilities
- Authentication and authorization flaws
- Data exposure risks
- Dependency vulnerabilities
- Configuration security issues

# Hoja de referencia · OpenCode 1.18.25

## Dónde puede haber configuración

Según la documentación de esta versión, las fuentes se cargan en este orden, y las posteriores reemplazan a las anteriores **sólo en las claves en conflicto** (los archivos se combinan, no se reemplazan enteros):

1. Configuración remota de la organización (`.well-known/opencode`)
2. Configuración global: `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`
3. Archivo indicado por la variable de entorno `OPENCODE_CONFIG`
4. Configuración del proyecto: `opencode.json`
5. Directorios `.opencode/`
6. Configuración indicada en la variable de entorno `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`
7. Archivos de configuración administrada
8. Preferencias administradas de macOS

OpenCode busca el `opencode.json` del proyecto en el directorio actual y sube hasta la raíz del repositorio git.

Un valor puede tomarse de una variable de entorno con `{env:NOMBRE}` o del contenido de un archivo con `{file:ruta}`.

## Dónde se declara cada cosa

| Qué | Dónde |
|---|---|
| Agentes | Clave `agent` de un `opencode.json`, o archivos markdown en `agents/` dentro de `~/.config/opencode/` o de `.opencode/` |
| Permisos | Clave `permission`, en el nivel superior o dentro de un agente |
| Comandos, skills, plugins | Subcarpetas `commands/`, `skills/`, `plugins/` dentro de `~/.config/opencode/` o de `.opencode/` |

Valores posibles de un permiso: `allow` (se ejecuta sin aprobación) · `ask` (se pide aprobación) · `deny` (se bloquea).

## Comandos disponibles

| Comando | Qué hace (según `--help`) |
|---|---|
| `opencode debug config` | Muestra la configuración resuelta |
| `opencode debug agent <nombre>` | Muestra los detalles de configuración de un agente |
| `opencode debug skill` | Lista las skills disponibles. Incluye `customize-opencode`, una skill de la propia herramienta sobre su configuración |
| `opencode debug paths` | Muestra las rutas globales (datos, configuración, caché, estado) |
| `opencode agent list` | Lista los agentes disponibles |
| `opencode --help` · `opencode debug --help` | Lista todos los comandos y subcomandos |

## Documentación

Documentación oficial de OpenCode 1.18.25, en inglés y sin conexión: abrí en el navegador `~/Documentacion-OpenCode/index.html`. Se puede buscar dentro de cada página con Ctrl+F.

Introduction

70:

export const console = config.console

71:

OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent. It's available as a terminal-based interface, desktop app, or IDE extension.

72:

73:

Let's get started.

74:
75:

Prerequisites

76:

To use OpenCode in your terminal, you'll need:

77:
    78:
  1. 79:

    A modern terminal emulator like: 80: - WezTerm, cross-platform 81: - Alacritty, cross-platform 82: - Ghostty, Linux and macOS 83: - Kitty, Linux and macOS

    84:
    2. 85:

    API keys for the LLM providers you want to use.

    87:
    3. 88:
89:
90:

Install

91:

The easiest way to install OpenCode is through the install script.

92: 
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
93:
94:

You can also install it with the following commands:

95:
    96:
  • Using Node.js
    • 97:
98:
npm
99: 100: 
  ```bash
101:   npm install -g opencode-ai
102:   ```
103:
104:
Bun
105: 106: 
    ```bash
107:     bun install -g opencode-ai
108:     ```
109:
110:
pnpm
111: 112: 
    ```bash
113:     pnpm install -g opencode-ai
114:     ```
115:
116:
Yarn
117: 118: 
    ```bash
119:     yarn global add opencode-ai
120:     ```
121:
122:
    123:
  • Using Homebrew on macOS and Linux
    • 124:
125:

bash 126: brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode

127:
128:

We recommend using the OpenCode tap for the most up to date releases. The official brew install opencode formula is maintained by the Homebrew team and is updated less frequently.

129:
130:
    131:
  • Installing on Arch Linux
    • 132:
133:

bash 134: sudo pacman -S opencode # Arch Linux (Stable) 135: paru -S opencode-bin # Arch Linux (Latest from AUR)

136:

Windows

137:
138:
Recommended: Use WSL
139:

For the best experience on Windows, we recommend using Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). It provides better performance and full compatibility with OpenCode's features.

140:
141:
    142:
  • Using Chocolatey
    • 143:
144:

bash 145: choco install opencode

146:
    147:
  • Using Scoop
    • 148:
149:

bash 150: scoop install opencode

151:
    152:
  • Using NPM
    • 153:
154:

bash 155: npm install -g opencode-ai

156:
    157:
  • Using Mise
    • 158:
159:

bash 160: mise use -g github:anomalyco/opencode

161:
    162:
  • Using Docker
    • 163:
164:

bash 165: docker run -it --rm ghcr.io/anomalyco/opencode

166:

Support for installing OpenCode on Windows using Bun is currently in progress.

167:

You can also grab the binary from the Releases.

168:
169:

Configure

170:

With OpenCode you can use any LLM provider by configuring their API keys.

171:

If you are new to using LLM providers, we recommend using OpenCode Zen. 172: It's a curated list of models that have been tested and verified by the OpenCode 173: team.

174:
    175:

    2. 176:
177:

txt 178: /connect

179:
    180:

    182:
    2. 183:
  2. 184:

txt 188: ┌ API key 189: │ 190: │ 191: └ enter

Alternatively, you can select one of the other providers. Learn more.

193:
194:

Initialize

195:

Now that you've configured a provider, you can navigate to a project that 196: you want to work on.

197: 
cd /path/to/project
198:
199:

And run OpenCode.

200: 
opencode
201:
202:

Next, initialize OpenCode for the project by running the following command.

203: 
/init
204:
205:

This will get OpenCode to analyze your project and create an AGENTS.md file in 206: the project root.

207:
208:
Tip
209:

You should commit your project's AGENTS.md file to Git.

210:
211:

This helps OpenCode understand the project structure and the coding patterns 212: used.

213:
214:

Usage

215:

You are now ready to use OpenCode to work on your project. Feel free to ask it 216: anything!

217:

If you are new to using an AI coding agent, here are some examples that might 218: help.

219:
220:

Ask questions

221:

You can ask OpenCode to explain the codebase to you.

222:
223:
Tip
224:

Use the @ key to fuzzy search for files in the project.

225:
226: 
How is authentication handled in @packages/functions/src/api/index.ts
227:
228:

This is helpful if there's a part of the codebase that you didn't work on.

229:
230:

Add features

231:

You can ask OpenCode to add new features to your project. Though we first recommend asking it to create a plan.

232:
    233:
  1. Create a plan
    2. 234:
235:

OpenCode has a Plan mode that disables its ability to make changes and 236: instead suggest how it'll implement the feature.

237:

Switch to it using the Tab key. You'll see an indicator for this in the lower right corner.

238:

bash 239: <TAB>

240:

Now let's describe what we want it to do.

241:

txt 242: When a user deletes a note, we'd like to flag it as deleted in the database. 243: Then create a screen that shows all the recently deleted notes. 244: From this screen, the user can undelete a note or permanently delete it.

245:

You want to give OpenCode enough details to understand what you want. It helps 246: to talk to it like you are talking to a junior developer on your team.

247:
248:
Tip
249:

Give OpenCode plenty of context and examples to help it understand what you 250: want.

251:
252:
    253:
  1. Iterate on the plan
    2. 254:
255:

Once it gives you a plan, you can give it feedback or add more details.

256:

txt 257: We'd like to design this new screen using a design I've used before. 258: [Image #1] Take a look at this image and use it as a reference.

259:
260:
Tip
261:

Drag and drop images into the terminal to add them to the prompt.

262:
263:

OpenCode can scan any images you give it and add them to the prompt. You can 264: do this by dragging and dropping an image into the terminal.

265:
    266:
  1. Build the feature
    2. 267:
268:

Once you feel comfortable with the plan, switch back to Build mode by 269: hitting the Tab key again.

270:

bash 271: <TAB>

272:

And asking it to make the changes.

273:

bash 274: Sounds good! Go ahead and make the changes.

275:
276:

Make changes

277:

For more straightforward changes, you can ask OpenCode to directly build it 278: without having to review the plan first.

279: 
We need to add authentication to the /settings route. Take a look at how this is
280: handled in the /notes route in @packages/functions/src/notes.ts and implement
281: the same logic in @packages/functions/src/settings.ts
282:
283:

You want to make sure you provide a good amount of detail so OpenCode makes the right 284: changes.

285:
286:

Undo changes

287:

Let's say you ask OpenCode to make some changes.

288: 
Can you refactor the function in @packages/functions/src/api/index.ts?
289:
290:

But you realize that it is not what you wanted. You can undo the changes 291: using the /undo command.

292: 
/undo
293:
294:

OpenCode will now revert the changes you made and show your original message 295: again.

296: 
Can you refactor the function in @packages/functions/src/api/index.ts?
297:
298:

From here you can tweak the prompt and ask OpenCode to try again.

299:
300:
Tip
301:

You can run /undo multiple times to undo multiple changes.

302:
303:

Or you can redo the changes using the /redo command.

304: 
/redo
305:
306:
307:

Share

308:

OpenCode 1.18.25 docs Introduction ACP Support Agent Skills Agents CLI Commands Config Custom Tools Ecosystem Enterprise Formatters GitHub GitLab Go IDE Keybinds LSP Servers MCP servers Models Network Permissions Plugins Policies Providers References Rules SDK Server Share Themes Tools Troubleshooting TUI Web Windows (WSL) Zen

Introduction

export const console = config.console

OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent. It's available as a terminal-based interface, desktop app, or IDE extension.

Let's get started.

Prerequisites

To use OpenCode in your terminal, you'll need:

  1. A modern terminal emulator like: - WezTerm, cross-platform - Alacritty, cross-platform - Ghostty, Linux and macOS - Kitty, Linux and macOS

  2. API keys for the LLM providers you want to use.

Install

The easiest way to install OpenCode is through the install script.

curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash

You can also install it with the following commands:

  • Using Node.js
npm
  ```bash
  npm install -g opencode-ai
  ```
Bun
    ```bash
    bun install -g opencode-ai
    ```
pnpm
    ```bash
    pnpm install -g opencode-ai
    ```
Yarn
    ```bash
    yarn global add opencode-ai
    ```
  • Using Homebrew on macOS and Linux

bash brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode

We recommend using the OpenCode tap for the most up to date releases. The official brew install opencode formula is maintained by the Homebrew team and is updated less frequently.

  • Installing on Arch Linux

bash sudo pacman -S opencode # Arch Linux (Stable) paru -S opencode-bin # Arch Linux (Latest from AUR)

Windows

Recommended: Use WSL

For the best experience on Windows, we recommend using Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). It provides better performance and full compatibility with OpenCode's features.

  • Using Chocolatey

bash choco install opencode

  • Using Scoop

bash scoop install opencode

  • Using NPM

bash npm install -g opencode-ai

  • Using Mise

bash mise use -g github:anomalyco/opencode

  • Using Docker

bash docker run -it --rm ghcr.io/anomalyco/opencode

Support for installing OpenCode on Windows using Bun is currently in progress.

You can also grab the binary from the Releases.

Configure

With OpenCode you can use any LLM provider by configuring their API keys.

If you are new to using LLM providers, we recommend using OpenCode Zen. It's a curated list of models that have been tested and verified by the OpenCode team.

  1. Run the /connect command in the TUI, select opencode, and head to opencode.ai/auth.

txt /connect

  1. Sign in, add your billing details, and copy your API key.

  2. Paste your API key.

txt ┌ API key │ │ └ enter

Alternatively, you can select one of the other providers. Learn more.

Initialize

Now that you've configured a provider, you can navigate to a project that you want to work on.

cd /path/to/project

And run OpenCode.

opencode

Next, initialize OpenCode for the project by running the following command.

/init

This will get OpenCode to analyze your project and create an AGENTS.md file in the project root.

Tip

You should commit your project's AGENTS.md file to Git.

This helps OpenCode understand the project structure and the coding patterns used.

Usage

You are now ready to use OpenCode to work on your project. Feel free to ask it anything!

If you are new to using an AI coding agent, here are some examples that might help.

Ask questions

You can ask OpenCode to explain the codebase to you.

Tip

Use the @ key to fuzzy search for files in the project.

How is authentication handled in @packages/functions/src/api/index.ts

This is helpful if there's a part of the codebase that you didn't work on.

Add features

You can ask OpenCode to add new features to your project. Though we first recommend asking it to create a plan.

  1. Create a plan

OpenCode has a Plan mode that disables its ability to make changes and instead suggest how it'll implement the feature.

Switch to it using the Tab key. You'll see an indicator for this in the lower right corner.

bash <TAB>

Now let's describe what we want it to do.

txt When a user deletes a note, we'd like to flag it as deleted in the database. Then create a screen that shows all the recently deleted notes. From this screen, the user can undelete a note or permanently delete it.

You want to give OpenCode enough details to understand what you want. It helps to talk to it like you are talking to a junior developer on your team.

Tip

Give OpenCode plenty of context and examples to help it understand what you want.

  1. Iterate on the plan

Once it gives you a plan, you can give it feedback or add more details.

txt We'd like to design this new screen using a design I've used before. [Image #1] Take a look at this image and use it as a reference.

Tip

Drag and drop images into the terminal to add them to the prompt.

OpenCode can scan any images you give it and add them to the prompt. You can do this by dragging and dropping an image into the terminal.

  1. Build the feature

Once you feel comfortable with the plan, switch back to Build mode by hitting the Tab key again.

bash <TAB>

And asking it to make the changes.

bash Sounds good! Go ahead and make the changes.

Make changes

For more straightforward changes, you can ask OpenCode to directly build it without having to review the plan first.

We need to add authentication to the /settings route. Take a look at how this is
handled in the /notes route in @packages/functions/src/notes.ts and implement
the same logic in @packages/functions/src/settings.ts

You want to make sure you provide a good amount of detail so OpenCode makes the right changes.

Undo changes

Let's say you ask OpenCode to make some changes.

Can you refactor the function in @packages/functions/src/api/index.ts?

But you realize that it is not what you wanted. You can undo the changes using the /undo command.

/undo

OpenCode will now revert the changes you made and show your original message again.

Can you refactor the function in @packages/functions/src/api/index.ts?

From here you can tweak the prompt and ask OpenCode to try again.

Tip

You can run /undo multiple times to undo multiple changes.

Or you can redo the changes using the /redo command.

/redo

Share

The conversations that you have with OpenCode can be shared with your team.

/share

This will create a link to the current conversation and copy it to your clipboard.

Note

Conversations are not shared by default.

Here's an example conversation with OpenCode.

Customize

And that's it! You are now a pro at using OpenCode.

To make it your own, we recommend picking a theme, customizing the keybinds, configuring code formatters, creating custom commands, or playing around with the OpenCode config.

However, there are only a few of them that are good at both generating code and tool calling.

Here are several models that work well with OpenCode, in no particular order. (This is not an exhaustive list nor is it necessarily up to date):

  • GPT 5.2

Configure models

You can globally configure a model's options through the config.

{

          "options": {

            },
          },
        },
      },
    },
  },

Here we're configuring global settings for two built-in models: gpt-5 when accessed via the openai provider, and claude-sonnet-4-20250514 when accessed via the anthropic provider. The built-in provider and model names can be found on Models.dev.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",

    "opencode": {

            "low": {
              "reasoningEffort": "low",

Precedence order

95:

Config sources are loaded in this order (later sources override earlier ones):

96:
    97:
  1. Remote config (from .well-known/opencode) - organizational defaults
    2. 98:
  2. Global config (~/.config/opencode/opencode.json) - user preferences
    3. 99:
  3. Custom config (OPENCODE_CONFIG env var) - custom overrides
    4. 100:
  4. Project config (opencode.json in project) - project-specific settings
    5. 101:
  5. .opencode directories - agents, commands, plugins
    6. 102:
  6. Inline config (OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT env var) - runtime overrides
    7. 103:
  7. Managed config files (/Library/Application Support/opencode/ on macOS) - admin-controlled
    8. 104:
  8. macOS managed preferences (.mobileconfig via MDM) - highest priority, not user-overridable
    9. 105:
106:

This means project configs can override global defaults, and global configs can override remote organizational defaults. Managed settings override everything.

107:
108:
Note
109:

The .opencode and ~/.config/opencode directories use plural names for subdirectories: agents/, commands/, modes/, plugins/, skills/, tools/, and themes/. Singular names (e.g., agent/) are also supported for backwards compatibility.

110:
111:
112:

Remote

113:

Organizations can provide default configuration via the .well-known/opencode endpoint. This is fetched automatically when you authenticate with a provider that supports it.

114:

Remote config is loaded first, serving as the base layer. All other config sources (global, project) can override these defaults.

115:

For example, if your organization provides MCP servers that are disabled by default:

116: 
{
117:   "mcp": {
118:     "jira": {
119:       "type": "remote",
120:       "url": "https://jira.example.com/mcp",
121:       "enabled": false
122:     }
123:   }
124: }
125:
126:

You can enable specific servers in your local config:

127: 
{
128:   "mcp": {
129:     "jira": {
130:       "type": "remote",
131:       "url": "https://jira.example.com/mcp",
132:       "enabled": true
133:     }
134:   }
135: }
136:
137:
138:

Global

139:

Place your global OpenCode config in ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json. Use global config for user-wide server/runtime preferences like providers, models, and permissions.

140:

For TUI-specific settings, use ~/.config/opencode/tui.json.

141:

Global config overrides remote organizational defaults.

142:
143:

Per project

144:

Add opencode.json in your project root. Project config has the highest precedence among standard config files - it overrides both global and remote configs.

145:

For project-specific TUI settings, add tui.json alongside it.

146:
147:
Tip
148:

Place project specific config in the root of your project.

149:
150:

When OpenCode starts up, it first looks for a config file in the current directory, then traverses up to the nearest Git directory.

151:

This is also safe to be checked into Git and uses the same schema as the global one.

152:
153:

Custom path

154:

Specify a custom config file path using the OPENCODE_CONFIG environment variable.

155: 
export OPENCODE_CONFIG=/path/to/my/custom-config.json
156: opencode run "Hello world"
157:
158:

Custom config is loaded between global and project configs in the precedence order.

159:
160:

Custom directory

161:

Specify a custom config directory using the OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR 162: environment variable. This directory will be searched for agents, commands, 163: modes, and plugins just like the standard .opencode directory, and should 164: follow the same structure.

165: 
export OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR=/path/to/my/config-directory
166: opencode run "Hello world"
167:
168:

The custom directory is loaded after the global config and .opencode directories, so it can override their settings.

169:
170:

Managed settings

171:

Organizations can enforce configuration that users cannot override. Managed settings are loaded at the highest priority tier.

172:

File-based

173:

Drop an opencode.json or opencode.jsonc file in the system managed config directory:

174: 175: 176: 177: 178: 179: 180: 181: 182: 183: 184: 185: 186: 187: 188: 189: 190: 191: 192: 193: 194: 195:
PlatformPath
macOS/Library/Application Support/opencode/
Linux/etc/opencode/
Windows%ProgramData%\opencode
196:

These directories require admin/root access to write, so users cannot modify them.

197:

macOS managed preferences

198:

On macOS, OpenCode reads managed preferences from the ai.opencode.managed preference domain. Deploy a .mobileconfig via MDM (Jamf, Kandji, FleetDM) and the settings are enforced automatically.

199:

OpenCode checks these paths:

200:
    201:
  1. /Library/Managed Preferences/<user>/ai.opencode.managed.plist
    2. 202:
  2. /Library/Managed Preferences/ai.opencode.managed.plist
    3. 203:
204:

The plist keys map directly to opencode.json fields. MDM metadata keys (PayloadUUID, PayloadType, etc.) are stripped automatically.

205:

Creating a .mobileconfig

206:

Use the ai.opencode.managed PayloadType. The OpenCode config keys go directly in the payload dict:

207: 
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
208: <!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN"
209:   "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
210: <plist version="1.0">
211: <dict>
212:   <key>PayloadContent</key>
213:   <array>
214:     <dict>
215:       <key>PayloadType</key>
216:       <string>ai.opencode.managed</string>
217:       <key>PayloadIdentifier</key>
218:       <string>com.example.opencode.config</string>
219:       <key>PayloadUUID</key>
220:       <string>GENERATE-YOUR-OWN-UUID</string>
221:       <key>PayloadVersion</key>
222:       <integer>1</integer>
223:       <key>share</key>
224:       <string>disabled</string>
225:       <key>server</key>
226:       <dict>
227:         <key>hostname</key>
228:         <string>127.0.0.1</string>
229:       </dict>
230:       <key>permission</key>
231:       <dict>
232:         <key>*</key>
233:         <string>ask</string>
234:         <key>bash</key>
235:         <dict>
236:           <key>*</key>
237:           <string>ask</string>
238:           <key>rm -rf *</key>
239:           <string>deny</string>
240:         </dict>
241:       </dict>
242:     </dict>
243:   </array>
244:   <key>PayloadType</key>
245:   <string>Configuration</string>
246:   <key>PayloadIdentifier</key>
247:   <string>com.example.opencode</string>
248:   <key>PayloadUUID</key>
249:   <string>GENERATE-YOUR-OWN-UUID</string>
250:   <key>PayloadVersion</key>
251:   <integer>1</integer>
252: </dict>
253: </plist>
254:
255:

Generate unique UUIDs with uuidgen. Customize the settings to match your organization's requirements.

256:

Deploying via MDM

257:
    258:
  • Jamf Pro: Computers > Configuration Profiles > Upload > scope to target devices or smart groups
    • 259:
  • FleetDM: Add the .mobileconfig to your gitops repo under mdm.macos_settings.custom_settings and run fleetctl apply
    • 260:
261:

Verifying on a device

262:

Double-click the .mobileconfig to install locally for testing (shows in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Profiles), then run:

263: 
opencode debug config
264:
265:

All managed preference keys appear in the resolved config and cannot be overridden by user or project configuration.

267:

Schema

268:

The server/runtime config schema is defined in opencode.ai/config.json.

269:

TUI config uses opencode.ai/tui.json.

270:

Your editor should be able to validate and autocomplete based on the schema.

271:
272:

TUI

273:

Use a dedicated tui.json (or tui.jsonc) file for TUI-specific settings.

274: 
{
275:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/tui.json",
276:   "scroll_speed": 3,
277:   "scroll_acceleration": {
278:     "enabled": true
279:   },
280:   "diff_style": "auto",
281:   "cursor": {
282:     "style": "block",
283:     "blinking": true
284:   },
285:   "mouse": true,
286:   "attention": {
287:     "enabled": true,
288:     "notifications": true,
289:     "sound": true,
290:     "volume": 0.4
291:   }
292: }
293:
294:

Use OPENCODE_TUI_CONFIG to point to a custom TUI config file.

295:

When cursor.style is "default", the terminal default cursor is restored, so cursor.blinking has no effect.

296:

Set attention.enabled to turn on TUI desktop notifications and sounds. See TUI attention.

297:

Legacy theme, keybinds, and tui keys in opencode.json are deprecated and automatically migrated when possible.

298:
299:

Server

300:

You can configure server settings for the opencode serve and opencode web commands through the server option.

301: 
{
302:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
303:   "server": {
304:     "port": 4096,
305:     "hostname": "0.0.0.0",
306:     "mdns": true,
307:     "mdnsDomain": "myproject.local",
308:     "cors": ["http://localhost:5173"]
309:   }
310: }
311:
312:

Available options:

313:
    314:
  • port - Port to listen on.
    • 315:
  • hostname - Hostname to listen on. When mdns is enabled and no hostname is set, defaults to 0.0.0.0.
    • 316:
  • mdns - Enable mDNS service discovery. This allows other devices on the network to discover your OpenCode server.
    • 317:
  • mdnsDomain - Custom domain name for mDNS service. Defaults to opencode.local. Useful for running multiple instances on the same network.
    • 318:
  • cors - Additional origins to allow for CORS when using the HTTP server from a browser-based client. Values must be full origins (scheme + host + optional port), eg https://app.example.com.
    • 319:
320:

Learn more about the server here.

321:
322:

Shell

323:

You can configure the shell used for the interactive terminal using the shell option. Compatible shells are also used for agent tool calls.

324: 
{
325:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
326:   "shell": "pwsh"
327: }
328:
329:

If not specified, OpenCode will automatically discover and use a sensible default based on your operating system (e.g. pwsh or cmd.exe on Windows, /bin/zsh or /bin/bash on macOS/Linux). You can provide an absolute path or a short name.

330:
331:

Tools

332:

You can manage the tools an LLM can use through the tools option.

333: 
{
334:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
335:   "tools": {
336:     "write": false,
337:     "bash": false
338:   }
339: }
340:
341:

Learn more about tools here.

342:
343:

Models

344:

You can configure the providers and models you want to use in your OpenCode config through the provider, model and small_model options.

345: 
{
346:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
347:   "provider": {},
348:   "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5",
349:   "small_model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"
350: }
351:
352:

The small_model option configures a separate model for lightweight tasks like title generation. By default, OpenCode tries to use a cheaper model if one is available from your provider, otherwise it falls back to your main model.

353:

Provider options can include timeout, chunkTimeout, and setCacheKey:

354: 
{
355:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
356:   "provider": {
357:     "anthropic": {
358:       "options": {
359:         "timeout": 600000,
360:         "chunkTimeout": 30000,
361:         "setCacheKey": true
362:       }
363:     }
364:   }
365: }
366:
367:
    368:
  • timeout - Request timeout in milliseconds (default: 300000). Set to false to disable.
    • 369:
  • chunkTimeout - Timeout in milliseconds between streamed response chunks. If no chunk arrives in time, the request is aborted.
    • 370:
  • setCacheKey - Ensure a cache key is always set for designated provider.
    • 371:
372:

You can also configure local models. Learn more.

373:
374:

Policies

375:

Use the experimental.policies option to allow or deny OpenCode actions on configured resources. Currently, policies can control which providers OpenCode may use.

376: 
{
377:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
378:   "experimental": {
379:     "policies": [
380:       {
381:         "effect": "deny",
382:         "action": "provider.use",
383:         "resource": "openai"
384:       }
385:     ]
386:   }
387: }
388:
389:

Learn more about policies here.

390:
391:

Image attachments

392:

OpenCode normalizes image attachments before sending them to the model. By default, images are resized when they exceed 2000x2000 pixels or 5242880 base64 bytes.

393:

Configure image attachment limits with the attachment.image option:

394: 
{
395:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
396:   "attachment": {
397:     "image": {
398:       "auto_resize": true,
399:       "max_width": 2000,
400:       "max_height": 2000,
401:       "max_base64_bytes": 5242880
402:     }
403:   }
404: }
405:
406:
    407:
  • auto_resize - Resize images that exceed the configured limits before provider requests. Set to false to reject oversized images instead.
    • 408:
  • max_width - Maximum image width in pixels before resizing or rejection.
    • 409:
  • max_height - Maximum image height in pixels before resizing or rejection.
    • 410:
  • max_base64_bytes - Maximum encoded image payload size. This is the base64 payload size, not the original file size.
    • 411:
412:

If an image still cannot fit after resizing, OpenCode omits oversized tool-result images or fails oversized user-provided images with an image size error.

414:

Provider-Specific Options

415:

Some providers support additional configuration options beyond the generic timeout and apiKey settings.

416:
Amazon Bedrock
417:

Amazon Bedrock supports AWS-specific configuration:

418: 
{
419:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
420:   "provider": {
421:     "amazon-bedrock": {
422:       "options": {
423:         "region": "us-east-1",
424:         "profile": "my-aws-profile",
425:         "endpoint": "https://bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.vpce-xxxxx.amazonaws.com"
426:       }
427:     }
428:   }
429: }
430:
431:
    432:
  • region - AWS region for Bedrock (defaults to AWS_REGION env var or us-east-1)
    • 433:
  • profile - AWS named profile from ~/.aws/credentials (defaults to AWS_PROFILE env var)
    • 434:
  • endpoint - Custom endpoint URL for VPC endpoints. This is an alias for the generic baseURL option using AWS-specific terminology. If both are specified, endpoint takes precedence.
    • 435:
436:
437:
Note
438:

Bearer tokens (AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK or /connect) take precedence over profile-based authentication. See authentication precedence for details.

439:
440:

Learn more about Amazon Bedrock configuration.

Themes

Set your UI theme in tui.json.

{

Agents

452:

You can configure specialized agents for specific tasks through the agent option.

453: 
{
454:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
455:   "agent": {
456:     "code-reviewer": {
457:       "description": "Reviews code for best practices and potential issues",
458:       "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5",
459:       "prompt": "You are a code reviewer. Focus on security, performance, and maintainability.",
460:       "tools": {
461:         // Disable file modification tools for review-only agent
462:         "write": false,
463:         "edit": false,
464:       },
465:     },
466:   },
467: }
468:
469:

You can also define agents using markdown files in ~/.config/opencode/agents/ or .opencode/agents/. Learn more here.

470:
471:

Default agent

472:

You can set the default agent using the default_agent option. This determines which agent is used when none is explicitly specified.

473: 
{
474:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
475:   "default_agent": "plan"
476: }
477:
478:

The default agent must be a primary agent (not a subagent). This can be a built-in agent like "build" or "plan", or a custom agent you've defined. If the specified agent doesn't exist or is a subagent, OpenCode will fall back to "build" with a warning.

479:

This setting applies across all interfaces: TUI, CLI (opencode run), desktop app, and GitHub Action.

480:
481:

Subagent depth

482:

You can control how deeply subagents can invoke other subagents using the subagent_depth option.

483: 
{
484:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
485:   "subagent_depth": 2
486: }
487:
488:

The default is 1, which allows primary agents to launch subagents but prevents those subagents from launching additional subagents. Set it to 2 to allow one additional level of nested subagents, or 0 to prevent all subagent launches.

489:
490:

Sharing

491:

You can configure the share feature through the share option.

492: 
{
493:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
494:   "share": "manual"
495: }
496:
497:

This takes:

498:
    499:
  • "manual" - Allow manual sharing via commands (default)
    • 500:
  • "auto" - Automatically share new conversations
    • 501:
  • "disabled" - Disable sharing entirely
    • 502:
503:

By default, sharing is set to manual mode where you need to explicitly share conversations using the /share command.

504:
505:

Commands

506:

You can configure custom commands for repetitive tasks through the command option.

507: 
{
508:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
509:   "command": {
510:     "test": {
511:       "template": "Run the full test suite with coverage report and show any failures.\nFocus on the failing tests and suggest fixes.",
512:       "description": "Run tests with coverage",
513:       "agent": "build",
514:       "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5",
515:     },
516:     "component": {
517:       "template": "Create a new React component named $ARGUMENTS with TypeScript support.\nInclude proper typing and basic structure.",
518:       "description": "Create a new component",
519:     },
520:   },
521: }
522:
523:

You can also define commands using markdown files in ~/.config/opencode/commands/ or .opencode/commands/. Learn more here.

524:
525:

Keybinds

526:

Customize TUI keyboard shortcuts in tui.json with keybinds.

527: 
{
528:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/tui.json",
529:   "keybinds": {
530:     "command_list": "ctrl+p"
531:   }
532: }
533:
534:

keybinds is merged with built-in defaults, so you only need to configure the shortcuts you want to change.

535:

Learn more here.

536:
537:

Snapshot

538:

OpenCode uses snapshots to track file changes during agent operations, enabling you to undo and revert changes within a session. Snapshots are enabled by default.

539:

For large repositories or projects with many submodules, the snapshot system can cause slow indexing and significant disk usage as it tracks all changes using an internal git repository. You can disable snapshots using the snapshot option.

540: 
{
541:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
542:   "snapshot": false
543: }
544:
545:

Note that disabling snapshots means changes made by the agent cannot be rolled back through the UI.

546:
547:

Autoupdate

548:

OpenCode will automatically download any new updates when it starts up. You can disable this with the autoupdate option.

549: 
{
550:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
551:   "autoupdate": false
552: }
553:
554:

If you don't want updates but want to be notified when a new version is available, set autoupdate to "notify". 555: Notice that this only works if it was not installed using a package manager such as Homebrew.

Formatters

558:

You can enable and configure code formatters through the formatter option. Omit it to keep formatters disabled.

559: 
{
560:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
561:   "formatter": true
562: }
563:
564:

Use an object to keep built-ins enabled while configuring overrides or custom formatters.

565: 
{
566:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
567:   "formatter": {
568:     "prettier": {
569:       "disabled": true
570:     },
571:     "custom-prettier": {
572:       "command": ["npx", "prettier", "--write", "$FILE"],
573:       "environment": {
574:         "NODE_ENV": "development"
575:       },
576:       "extensions": [".js", ".ts", ".jsx", ".tsx"]
577:     }
578:   }
579: }
580:
581:

Learn more about formatters here.

You can enable and configure LSP servers through the lsp option. Omit it to keep LSP disabled.

{

603:

By default, opencode allows all operations without requiring explicit approval. You can change this using the permission option.

604:

For example, to ensure that the edit and bash tools require user approval:

605: 
{
606:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
607:   "permission": {
608:     "edit": "ask",

610:   }

Compaction

616:

You can control context compaction behavior through the compaction option.

617: 
{
618:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
619:   "compaction": {
620:     "auto": true,
621:     "prune": false,
622:     "reserved": 10000
623:   }
624: }
625:
626:
    627:
  • auto - Automatically compact the session when context is full (default: true).
    • 628:
  • prune - Remove old tool outputs to save tokens (default: false). Set to true to enable pruning.
    • 629:
  • reserved - Token buffer for compaction. Leaves enough window to avoid overflow during compaction.
    • 630:

Watcher

633:

You can configure file watcher ignore patterns through the watcher option.

634: 
{
635:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
636:   "watcher": {
637:     "ignore": ["node_modules/**", "dist/**", ".git/**"]
638:   }
639: }

Patterns follow glob syntax. Use this to exclude noisy directories from file watching.

MCP servers

You can configure MCP servers you want to use through the mcp option.

645: 
{

Plugins

653:

Plugins extend OpenCode with custom tools, hooks, and integrations.

654:

Place plugin files in .opencode/plugins/ or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/. You can also load plugins from npm through the plugin option.

655: 
{
656:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
657:   "plugin": ["opencode-helicone-session", "@my-org/custom-plugin"]
658: }

660:

Learn more here.

Instructions

663:

You can configure the instructions for the model you're using through the instructions option.

664: 
{
665:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
666:   "instructions": ["CONTRIBUTING.md", "docs/guidelines.md", ".cursor/rules/*.md"]
667: }
668:
669:

This takes an array of paths and glob patterns to instruction files. Learn more 670: about rules here.

671:
672:

Disabled providers

673:

You can disable providers that are loaded automatically through the disabled_providers option. This is useful when you want to prevent certain providers from being loaded even if their credentials are available.

674: 
{
675:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
676:   "disabled_providers": ["openai", "gemini"]
677: }
678:
679:
680:
Note
681:

The disabled_providers takes priority over enabled_providers.

682:
683:

The disabled_providers option accepts an array of provider IDs. When a provider is disabled:

684:
    685:
  • It won't be loaded even if environment variables are set.
    • 686:
  • It won't be loaded even if API keys are configured through the /connect command.
    • 687:
  • The provider's models won't appear in the model selection list.
    • 688:
689:
690:

Enabled providers

691:

You can specify an allowlist of providers through the enabled_providers option. When set, only the specified providers will be enabled and all others will be ignored.

692: 
{
693:   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
694:   "enabled_providers": ["anthropic", "openai"]
695: }
696:
697:

This is useful when you want to restrict OpenCode to only use specific providers rather than disabling them one by one.

698:
699:
